elements.text: After working through a design for maintaining consistency given a disk full condition during a multi-table write (which only occurs with a tx write), I realized that this condition is already managed. Multi-table writes occur both concurrently and during ongoing reads, such as by validation/confirmation and also client/server queries. Full consistency is of course eventual, but all queries produce logical results even in the midst of multi-table writes. So when a single table fails to expand during a write, such as for disk full, all we need to do is stop and report it.

elements.text: Resolved this, just placed a
pause
event rebroadcast in the backup event handler in the case of a
wait_lock
event. The
wait_lock
signals that store write exclusivity was not obtained for a full second and will retry. Resending the
pause

event suspends any channels that may have missed it on the initial send. This does technically present a halting problem, since that back and forth can theoretically go on forever, but that's extremely unlikely. If it did for some reason happen, all that occurs is the backup is deferred until store close, which suspends all channels, resulting in backup obtaining the lock, completing the snapshot, and then close obtaining the lock. So a simple one line good solution to a tricky race condition.

The node object doesn't have the ability to stop itself, which is intentional - sort of a design forcing function. The node (console process) stops the node via keyboard command. This forces the implementation to deal rationally with things like network disconnect, disk full, and store corruption (for example).

When reviewing the handling of store corruption and disk full I decided that it would be good to slightly modify the
libbitcoin-network

stack to enable connect/accept suspension. Normally the connectors are allocated at startup and run in a callback loop, always attempting to maintain the configured number of connections. But for both backup and store full/fault conditions, we need to suspend this.

So I made those modifications, which were simple. The
connector
and
acceptor
classes are now constructed with a reference to an atomic bool, owned by
p2p

. This tells them to bypass connection attempts with a specific error code. Since certain errors result in a delayed retry (precluding tight loops on things like no internet or no addresses), this fits naturally into the design.

The node object doesn't have the ability to stop itself, which is intentional - sort of a design forcing function. The node (console process) stops the node via keyboard command. This forces the implementation to deal rationally with things like network disconnect, disk full, and store corruption (for example).

When reviewing the handling of store corruption and disk full I decided that it would be good to slightly modify the `libbitcoin-network` stack to enable connect/accept suspension. Normally the connectors are allocated at startup and run in a callback loop, always attempting to maintain the configured number of connections. But for both backup and store full/fault conditions, we need to suspend this.

So I made those modifications, which were simple. The `connector` and `acceptor` classes are now constructed with a reference to an atomic bool, owned by `p2p`. This tells them to bypass connection attempts with a specific error code. Since certain errors result in a delayed retry (precluding tight loops on things like no internet or no addresses), this fits naturally into the design.

elements.text: So now when there is a store fault, or a disk full, or a snapshot starting, the network stops connecting but the process remains alive. Resume from a disk full condition is currently a command line option. The store object now retains the state of each table, and provides a summary query to provide context for these operations. This is all working seamlessly at this point.

elements.text: Snapshots can of course also lead to disk full, however once there are two snapshots there is never any more size increase. All writes are first suspended, then the snapshot directories are rotated and the older one deleted. Since only headers are written, size never changes, so we can always snap once we have to written. However if the disk is full the snapshot just leaves behind the one value directory (which is why we rotate two). I've verified the snapshot disk full behavior as well.

elements.text: Also as you can see above, log system config. This is helpful since the log system allows for all or some categories to be compiled out, such that the messages are not even constructed. But this can be misleading if it's not clear in the log or at the console what options are both compiled and enabled. They can be toggled on the command line, if compiled in, which reflects in the log. But this allows us to see log levels from startup.

elements.text: The schedule/criteria for automated snapshots is implemented. This consists of two configuration options, both intervals - bytes and confirmations. The node can very rapidly obtain the byte sum of all store headers and bodies. This is checked for each block arrival and the difference from startup is obtained. When this exceeds configured it backs up and resets the startup value. This can lead to a larger than expected gap if the node is stopped and then started, though this is acceptable. If a snapshot is taken close to stop (which should be expected) then this is moot.
